lines.text: Καὶ ἡ βίβλος τοῦ Χάλεκ.

lines.en: The book containing the benefits of the stars in the elementary

sections.text:
1 Liber Palchi idem est sine dubio qui in cod. 11, f. 193 ss. servatur. Cur ἑρμη-
νευτής dictus sit non satis intellego.
2 Chamasus non alius esse videtur atque Hamza Ispahanensis (Ḥamza ben Alha-
san Alisfahâni) qui circa ann. 961, p. C. n. notissimam historiam scripsit (Hamzae
Ispahanensis annalium libri V, ed. Gottwaldt 1844 s.). Nam et astronomiae, ut
temporum rationis investigator, peritus fuit (cf. Albîrûnî, Chronology of ancient
nations, ed. Sachau, 1879, p. 61 s. et passim).
3 Isak ben Salomon Israeli, philosophus et medicus c. ann. 950 mortuus, medio
aevo apud gentes occidentis quoque celeberrimus fuit (Cf. Steinschneider, Die
hebräischen Uebersetz. des Mittelalters, t. I, § 223 s. [p. 338] et § 479 s. [755 sqq.].
Etsi a mysticis doctrinis non abhorruit (Steinschneider, § 227), astrologiam tamen
coluisse non videtur.
4 Quis Hermetis Trismegisti liber ita designetur incertum.
5 Agitur fortasse de libro quodam astrologico Sabaeorum Carrhensium in hebraï-
cam linguam translato, cf. Chwolsohn, Die Ssabier, t. I, p. 715, t. II, p. 464. “ Liber
Haranitarum”, (ktāvā d’hārānāiē) Syris quoque notus erat, cf. Payne-Smith, Lexic.
Syr. s. v., t. I, p. 1376. — Formam tamen Χαρανιώτ(ου ?), aliud innuere videtur.
6 De Vettio Valente ne plura hic verba faciamus, cf. Riess in Pauly-Wissowa,
Realenc., t. II, c. 1822, supra p. 79.
7 Cf. supra, p. 81, n. 1.
sections.en:
1 The book of Palchus is without doubt the same as that preserved in cod. 11, f. 193 ss. Why he is called an interpreter I do not quite understand.
2 Chamasus seems to be none other than Hamza Ispahanensis (Ḥamza ben Alhasan Alisfahâni) who around the year 961 A.D. wrote a very well-known history (Hamzae Ispahanensis annalium libri V, ed. Gottwaldt 1844 s.). For he was also skilled in astronomy, as an investigator of the reckoning of times (cf. Albîrûnî, Chronology of ancient nations, ed. Sachau, 1879, p. 61 s. and passim).
3 Isak ben Salomon Israeli, philosopher and physician who died around the year 950, was also very famous in the Middle Ages among the peoples of the West (Cf. Steinschneider, Die hebräischen Uebersetz. des Mittelalters, t. I, § 223 s. [p. 338] and § 479 s. [755 sqq.]. Although he did not shrink from mystical doctrines (Steinschneider, § 227), he does not seem to have cultivated astrology.
4 Which book of Hermes Trismegistus is thus designated is uncertain.
5 It is perhaps a question of a certain astrological book of the Sabians of Harran translated into the Hebrew language, cf. Chwolsohn, Die Ssabier, t. I, p. 715, t. II, p. 464. “The Book of the Harranians”, (ktāvā d’hārānāiē) was also known to the Syrians, cf. Payne-Smith, Lexic. Syr. s. v., t. I, p. 1376. — However, the form Χαρανιώτ(ου ?) seems to hint at something else.
6 Let us not say more words here about Vettius Valens, cf. Riess in Pauly-Wissowa, Realenc., t. II, c. 1822, above p. 79.
7 Cf. above, p. 81, n. 1.

summary.headline: Forbidden Astrological Books
summary.text: A catalogue of forbidden astrological books, including works attributed to Palchus, Chamasus, Isaac son of Solomon, Hermes, Vettius Valens, and Mashallah, with titles concerning commerce, retrogradations, depressions, stellar benefits, co-risings, astronomical mysteries, and accurate considerations.
